question: What is retinal detachment?
answer: Retinal detachment happens when your retina (a light-sensitive layer of tissue at the back of your eye) is pulled away from its normal position [nei_050_chunk_01]. There are three types: rhegmatogenous, tractional, and exudative [nei_050_chunk_01]. Any type of retinal detachment is a medical emergency [nei_050_chunk_01]. If you have symptoms of a detached retina, go to the eye doctor or the emergency room right away [nei_050_chunk_01]. Early treatment can help prevent permanent vision loss [nei_050_chunk_01]. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the most common type and occurs if there is a small tear or break in the retina [nei_050_chunk_01]. The gel-like fluid in the center of the eye (called vitreous) can get behind the retina, pushing it away from the back of the eye [nei_050_chunk_01]. Tractional retinal detachment happens if scar tissue on the retina pulls it away from the back of the eye [nei_050_chunk_02]. Exudative retinal detachment occurs when fluid builds up behind the retina without tears or breaks [nei_050_chunk_03]. This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: How do eye doctors check for RP?
answer: Eye doctors check for retinitis pigmentosa (RP) as part of a comprehensive dilated eye exam [nei_020_chunk_03] ◐. This involves using eye drops to dilate the pupil, allowing the doctor to examine the retina for signs of RP [nei_020_chunk_03] ◐. The exam also includes a visual field test to assess peripheral vision, which is often affected by RP [nei_020_chunk_03]. Additional tests may include electroretinography (ERG) to evaluate retinal response to light, optical coherence tomography (OCT) for detailed retinal imaging, and fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging using blue light [nei_020_chunk_03]. Genetic testing may also be recommended to determine the specific type of RP and its potential progression [nei_020_chunk_04]. This is general education, not a diagnosis.
